title: Building wearable health sensors with Northwestern professor Nabil Alshurafa
excerpt: How Northwestern's Nabil Alshurafa guides students to build ECG, PPG and motion-sensor prototypes, turn their own questions into hypotheses, and defend a research poster in ten days.
content:
Plenty of students headed for pre-med, computer science, or bioengineering can point to a health-monitoring app they built after a summer coding class. Far fewer have assembled a sensor, fought its signal noise, and watched it read a live heartbeat. That second kind of work is the focus of Northwestern University professor Nabil Alshurafa's track in CRI's Seoul Research Program: ten days of building wearable health sensors, collecting real physiological data, and turning students' own questions into a group research paper.

## Why the course starts with hardware

Applications from aspiring doctors and engineers tend to look alike. Students memorize disease mechanisms for biology class, then use the coding they already know to build a generic health app for a research report. Many sense the limits of that work: an app that only runs on a screen rarely comes close to preventing a real illness.

What top US universities and medical schools look for, in CRI's view, is intellectual vitality: students who connect the body's signals and behavior to hardware sensors, think through a system that could predict disease, and ask their own questions. The course is built to develop exactly that habit of mind.

## Who teaches it

Nabil Alshurafa earned his bachelor's, master's, and PhD at UCLA, studying computer science and artificial intelligence. He is a tenured associate professor at Northwestern, with appointments in Preventive Medicine at the Feinberg School of Medicine and in Computer Science and Electrical and Computer Engineering at the McCormick School of Engineering. He is also a Senior Member of the IEEE.

- **Wearables.** He has won several million dollars in research funding from the National Institutes of Health and leads large projects funded by the NIH and the National Science Foundation as principal investigator. He builds devices such as FaceBit, a smart face mask, and NeckSense, a necklace that tracks eating habits.
- **Behavior prediction.** His HABits Lab develops AI-based systems that use wearable sensor data to measure and predict behaviors such as stress, overeating, and poor posture.
- **Publications.** His research has appeared in leading journals and conferences, including *npj Digital Medicine*, ACM IMWUT, and IEEE BSN.

His students' track record speaks to his mentoring. The HABits Lab takes questions from undergraduates and interns as seriously as those from graduate students and develops them into papers and working devices. Students he has mentored have gone on to Northwestern's Feinberg School of Medicine, been recruited by the US National Security Agency, and founded healthcare startups of their own. Students who worry that their coding or questions are too basic will find a professor who knows how far a rough idea can go.

## Ten days as a junior researcher

For the length of the course, students work as the newest members of the lab. They build hardware prototypes and study how physiological data such as ECG (electrocardiography), PPG (photoplethysmography, which uses light to track blood flow), and stress-related signals arise in the body and how sensors capture them. Signal noise and hardware constraints can be frustrating at first. A few days in, the sensor system students assembled themselves is reading live biological data.

The larger aim is to understand mobile health (mHealth) as a system in which hardware, biological signals, and human behavior connect.

| Stage | What students do |
| --- | --- |
| Days 2–3 | Learn how wearable health sensors (ECG, PPG, motion) work and design their own hardware prototypes |
| Days 4–5 | Track physiological markers of stress, cardiovascular health, and metabolic health, and build a framework for turning them into sensor-based interventions |
| Day 7 | Analyze the collected data, connect it to patterns of behavior, and draw out meaningful health insights |
| Day 10 | Present and defend an academic poster of the group paper |

From there the course turns to preventive medicine: how could this data lead to preventive solutions for metabolic and cardiovascular disease? Students wear smartwatches and other devices to gather their own data and explore how stress, posture, caffeine, and exercise show up in their biosignals. Core topics include:

- Measuring stress, posture, sleep, and eating with wearable sensors, including heart rate variability (HRV) and galvanic skin response (GSR)
- Visualizing and statistically analyzing the data
- Designing machine-learning algorithms that predict behavior
- Team-based research design, experiments, paper writing, and poster presentation

Students also learn the basics of scientific writing and of institutional review boards (IRBs), design experiments with human participants, and practice handling medical and health data.

![Professor Alshurafa sits with three students in front of a projected slide listing study design, skeletal tracking, and an inertial measurement unit sensor](/editorial/224155738463-03.jpg "One student team's methods combined an IMU sensor with skeletal tracking.")

## From a hunch to a hypothesis

In a school science club, the topic is usually assigned, and it is usually the safe one. Here, research begins when students put their own questions on the table:

- How could everyday devices like smartphones or earbuds be repurposed as preventive health monitors?
- How do particular behavior patterns interact with the biological data that predict disease?
- How do environmental stressors such as heat waves or poor air quality affect the signals a wearable records?

After brainstorming, one question centered on mHealth systems becomes the team's research topic. Professor Alshurafa does not simply mark ideas right or wrong; he answers with a sharper question, something like: *To test that hypothesis, would ECG or a motion sensor give you better data? If signal noise creeps in, what does that do to the reliability of the whole system?* Working through follow-ups like these is how a vague curiosity becomes a hypothesis with solid engineering logic behind it.

![Professor Alshurafa and three students sit in front of a methods slide comparing an exercise group with a control group between two exams](/editorial/224155738463-01.jpg "One team's study compared running or meditating with scrolling on a phone between exams.")

## What students leave with

Teams build their sensors, analyze the data they collect, and draft and revise with close feedback until they have a finished group research paper with every member's name on it. The course produces four outputs:

1. **A group research paper.** Students write it with guidance from Professor Alshurafa and TAs from leading universities, and CRI supports each paper through submission to a journal or conference indexed in Scopus or CPCI.
2. **Research integrity.** Universities increasingly screen student research for plagiarism and AI ghostwriting, so CRI keeps similarity scores at or below 15% and verifies the data.
3. **An academic research poster.** Students learn to present complex technical work at a glance, the same skill 2025 students relied on at IEEE EMBS.
4. **A recommendation letter grounded in observation.** Over roughly 50 hours of class, Professor Alshurafa watches students assemble sensors and analyze data. Students who prove themselves can earn a letter that speaks to their individual abilities, contributions, and enthusiasm.

![A student types on a laptop showing a research paper draft in a shared document](/editorial/224262412735-04.jpg "Drafting and revising the team paper.")

## Poster day and what can follow

On Day 10, the paper becomes an academic poster. Students explain, in English, the sensor they designed, the data they collected, and the logic of their proposed interventions to Professor Alshurafa and other experts, then field their questions. It is the kind of defense graduate students go through, and strong preparation for college interviews.

The work does not have to end there:

- **Conferences.** Students who commit fully to the program are given the opportunity to take part in an IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBS) conference.
- **Competitions.** The hypotheses and prototypes can grow into entries for ISEF or the Conrad Challenge.
- **Internships.** A small number of students who show exceptional potential may be offered internships at healthcare startups or companies Professor Alshurafa is involved with.

In 2025, student teams from this class presented posters at IEEE EMBS BSN 2025, the International Conference on Body Sensor Networks. Their projects included:

- **Exercise and academic stress.** A comparison of running, meditation, and phone use as stress relief, measured with HRV and GSR, which found running the most effective.
- **TurtleTrack.** A neck-worn IMU device that detects poor posture and gives real-time feedback.
- **Caffeine and focus.** A study of how caffeine affects high school students' concentration, tracking HRV, heart rate, and GSR before and after caffeine intake.

Read the teams' story, and that of a student who built a runner's-knee rehabilitation wearable with Professor Alshurafa, on our [Student Success](/success) page.

![Two students stand at their research poster in a crowded conference hall while attendees look on](/editorial/224262412735-05.jpg "Seoul Research Program 2025 students presenting at an IEEE EMBS conference poster session.")

## Who the course suits

The 2026 track ran in person in Seoul from July 7 to 17, with Professor Alshurafa teaching on site for all ten days. It is designed for students interested in biology, medicine, biomedical engineering, electrical engineering, bioinformatics, or preventive medicine, and it suits those drawn to AI, psychology, and the life sciences as well. Basic coding knowledge is recommended. Groups are kept small so every student gets close mentoring and real time with the hardware.

Whatever their intended major, students practice defining a research problem, designing an experiment, and reasoning from data, and they gain a practical understanding of digital health technology. The project can also become part of their research portfolio for college applications.

Professor Alshurafa's course is one of the faculty-led tracks in CRI's summer research programs, where small groups work directly with visiting professors from leading universities. To see how the summer cohorts run and which tracks are open, explore the [Seoul and Global Research Programs](/research/summer-camp).

title: UCLA and UC Berkeley admit rates by major, and why research experience matters
excerpt: UC's fall 2024 data puts UCLA nursing at 1% and UC Berkeley public health at 2%. See the admit rates by major, and how three students used research to show fit with their majors.
content:
At UCLA, 5,790 students applied to study nursing and 55 were admitted: an admit rate of 1%. At UC Berkeley, public health admitted 62 of its 2,713 applicants. Numbers like these, now published by major for every University of California campus, show that the field you apply to can matter as much as the campus you choose.

The figures come from the UC Information Center, the university system's official data portal, which breaks down admissions by broad discipline across all nine undergraduate campuses. Depending on the campus and the field, admit rates differ by a factor of ten or more. So the useful question for UC applicants is no longer "Which campus is easiest?" but "Which major am I applying to, and what is my plan for getting in?" The data below covers applicants for the fall 2024 term.

## UC Berkeley: public health, computer science and business

UC Berkeley admitted 11% of its applicants overall. Its most selective field was public health, at 2%. Computer science and business came next at 4% each. At the other end of the range, arts and humanities admitted 23% of applicants, more than twice the campus rate.

| Broad discipline | Applicants | Admits | Admit rate | Admitted GPA (25th–75th percentile) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Public health | 2,713 | 62 | 2% | 4.14–4.30 |
| Computer science | 13,437 | 515 | 4% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Business | 8,069 | 327 | 4% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Architecture | 2,939 | 211 | 7% | 4.14–4.28 |
| Engineering | 21,831 | 1,698 | 8% | 4.21–4.30 |
| Social sciences | 18,816 | 1,683 | 9% | 4.16–4.29 |
| Other/interdisciplinary | 6,847 | 807 | 12% | 4.15–4.29 |
| Undeclared | 11,956 | 1,432 | 12% | 4.11–4.29 |
| Public administration | 260 | 33 | 13% | 4.11–4.26 |
| Physical sciences/math | 11,487 | 1,821 | 16% | 4.19–4.30 |
| Life sciences | 16,970 | 2,998 | 18% | 4.16–4.29 |
| Arts and humanities | 8,917 | 2,052 | 23% | 4.07–4.28 |
| **Campus overall** | 124,242 | 13,639 | 11% | 4.15–4.29 |

## UCLA: nursing, engineering and computer science

UCLA's overall admit rate was 9%, and nursing was its hardest major by a wide margin: 55 admits from 5,790 applicants. Engineering admitted 6% and computer science 4%, and in both fields the middle 50% of admitted students had GPAs starting at 4.25.

One detail deserves a closer look. Undeclared applicants were admitted at 7%, below the campus average, so treating "undeclared" as a back door into UCLA rarely works.

| Broad discipline | Applicants | Admits | Admit rate | Admitted GPA (25th–75th percentile) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Nursing | 5,790 | 55 | 1% | 4.25–4.30 |
| Computer science | 10,530 | 435 | 4% | 4.25–4.30 |
| Engineering | 22,301 | 1,329 | 6% | 4.25–4.32 |
| Education | 1,265 | 79 | 6% | 4.07–4.28 |
| Undeclared | 10,059 | 693 | 7% | 4.17–4.31 |
| Business | 13,634 | 1,110 | 8% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Arts and humanities | 15,133 | 1,244 | 8% | 4.04–4.29 |
| Social sciences | 23,884 | 2,234 | 9% | 4.17–4.30 |
| Other health science | 2,470 | 285 | 12% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Life sciences | 23,472 | 3,092 | 13% | 4.21–4.30 |
| Other/interdisciplinary | 4,591 | 597 | 13% | 4.21–4.30 |
| Public administration | 826 | 117 | 14% | 4.20–4.30 |
| Physical sciences/math | 12,316 | 1,844 | 15% | 4.22–4.32 |
| **Campus overall** | 146,272 | 13,114 | 9% | 4.20–4.30 |

## Four more campuses where the major changes the odds

The same pattern shows up at other popular campuses, though the gaps look different on each one.

| Admit rate | UC San Diego | UC Irvine | UC Davis | UC Santa Barbara |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Campus overall** | 27% | 29% | 42% | 33% |
| Computer science | 13% | 20% | 17% | 17% |
| Engineering | 17% | 28% | 38% | 21% |
| Business | 18% | 13% | 33% | 32% (435 applicants) |
| Life sciences | 36% | 34% | 51% | 40% |
| Physical sciences/math | 36% | 44% | 59% | 47% |
| Public health | 19% | 42% | — | — |
| Public administration | — | — | 67% (130 applicants) | — |

*A dash means the discipline is not listed for that campus.*

- **UC San Diego**'s numbers work in favor of strong students drawn to the basic sciences. Life sciences and physical sciences/math each admitted 36%, nearly three times the rate for computer science.
- **UC Irvine** is a textbook case of the major alone moving the odds: 13% in business and 20% in computer science, against 44% in physical sciences/math and 42% in public health.
- **UC Davis**, with a 42% overall rate, is the most attainable of these campuses for students whose interests fit, with 59% in physical sciences/math and 67% in public administration. Computer science, at 17%, is a different story.
- **UC Santa Barbara** admitted 33% overall, but only 17% in computer science and 21% in engineering, compared with 47% in physical sciences/math and 40% in life sciences.

## Why research keeps showing up in UC admits

Look at recent admits to UC Berkeley, UCLA and UC San Diego and a pattern is getting harder to miss. Grades alone are not what set them apart. What does is research experience tied directly to the intended major, a recommendation letter from a professor, and a tangible output such as a research paper. Three cases show how that plays out.

### UC Berkeley chemistry: a first paper on biomimetic nanomaterials

This student had been interested in chemistry and materials since high school. To show that fit more clearly, the student chose biomimetic nanomaterials as a research topic and worked with Professor Anish Tuteja of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. The project covered the full cycle, from reviewing the literature and structuring the study to interpreting the results and writing the paper. The outcome was a first research paper with the student's own name on it.

That research and the professor's recommendation letter became the core academic evidence in the student's application to chemistry at UC Berkeley, and the student was admitted.

### UCLA, Johns Hopkins and WashU: fluid dynamics for renewable energy

The second student was already at university, with energy systems and engineering as the target field, and worked with Professor Nasr Ghoniem of UCLA on applications of fluid dynamics in renewable energy systems. The project did not stop at summarizing theory. The student analyzed fluid flow inside actual energy systems and extended the work into a structural analysis of how efficiency changes.

![A student in a black T-shirt typing on a laptop at a café table](/editorial/224103498804-08.jpg "The second student, whose research applied fluid dynamics to renewable energy systems.")

The finished research and the accompanying recommendation letter supported applications to UCLA, Johns Hopkins University and Washington University in St. Louis. All three offered admission, and the student chose UCLA.

### UCSD, Stanford, Brown and Penn: wearables meet machine learning

The third student, also at university, was majoring in mechanical engineering but broadened that focus, setting out to combine wearable devices with machine learning. Working with Professor Nabil Alshurafa of Northwestern University, the student analyzed sensor data and applied pattern recognition and predictive models. The project brought mechanical engineering and AI together and ended as a complete research paper.

In later applications, that work was read as evidence of genuine interdisciplinary research, not just a record of completed coursework. The student received offers from several universities, including UC San Diego, Stanford, Brown and the University of Pennsylvania.

What these cases share is not simply hard work. It is activity that connects precisely to the intended major, and that is becoming a key factor in who gets in. For more students who built their applications around research, see the [Student Success](/success) page.

## Three questions to answer before you apply

Read closely, these admit rates are less a set of odds than a test of strategy. Before you apply, make sure you can answer three questions:

1. Which major am I applying to?
2. What have I done that connects directly to that major?
3. Do I have a substantial academic story that a recommender can write about in depth?

When all three line up, a UC admission stops being a matter of luck and becomes the result of a plan.

If you want research that matches the major you will list on your UC application, the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1) pairs you with a faculty mentor for an individually arranged project in your field, typically over two to four months.

title: Paper-writing guide, part 3: Figures are the face of your paper
excerpt: Editors and reviewers look at your figures before they read your text. Learn how to plan figures early, choose the right formats and tools, and design them for clarity.
content:
When you open a research paper, where do your eyes go first? Most readers skim the title and abstract, then jump straight to the figures, and editors and reviewers are no different. If the figures don't stand out, or look cluttered or clumsy, the paper can be rejected on the spot, before anyone properly reads the text.

That is why figures are the face of a paper. A single figure tells a reader how reliable the experiments are and how carefully the work was organized. This third part of CRI's seven-part paper-writing guide covers how researchers plan figures, which formats and tools they use, and the design principles that make a figure easy to understand.

## Why figures carry so much weight

In the natural sciences especially, the figures that visualize your results shape the first impression. A clean figure with an obvious main point says, "This study is well organized. It's worth reading." A messy one invites a reviewer to wonder how careful the experiments were, or to decide there is plenty of data but no clear message. One figure can color the verdict on the whole paper.

A figure is also more than a container for results. It is part of your argument, the place where you make your case visually. Good figures make a paper persuasive, and they are what get the text read.

## Plan your figures before you write

Figures are not supporting material you sketch at the last minute. They are closer to a blueprint for the whole paper.

When researchers start preparing a manuscript, the first thing they typically do is open PowerPoint and create a file called `Figure_v1`. Each figure gets its own slide. They drop in the key data and ask, "How should we show this?" Nothing has to be perfect yet; the point is to decide what role each figure will play in the overall story.

The slides then go to coauthors for feedback, and each revision is saved as a new version (`Figure_v2`, `Figure_v3`). This is where the real editorial calls get made: "We can drop this experiment," or "Let's shrink this into an inset."

The method works because the paper's structure forms around the figures. You learn which results are central and what needs emphasis, so by the time you start writing, the message of each section is already clear.

## Submission figures and publication figures are different

The format and resolution a journal expects at first submission are very different from what it asks for after acceptance.

**At initial submission**, keep it simple:

- Images embedded in your Word file are enough.
- High resolution isn't needed; figures just have to be easy to view in Word or PDF.
- Place each caption alongside its figure.
- JPEG, PNG, EMF or PDF files are all fine.

The goal is a tidy layout that lets editors and reviewers grasp the content quickly. There is no need to produce TIFF or AI files yet.

**After acceptance**, you resubmit your figures as high-resolution files that meet the journal's requirements. Journals commonly ask for these formats:

| Format | What it is used for |
| --- | --- |
| TIFF | The most common publication format, for photos and line art alike |
| AI / PDF | Vector-based, so text and lines never break up (typically made in Illustrator) |
| EPS / SVG | Line art and sketches; science journals sometimes require them |

Recommended resolution depends on the type of figure:

| Figure type | Resolution |
| --- | --- |
| Photo | 300 dpi |
| Mixed image | 600 dpi |
| Line art | 1,000 dpi |

Color mode matters too: **RGB** for online display, **CMYK** for print. In short, prepare each figure only to the standard its stage requires.

## Use vector formats wherever you can

File format is the single biggest technical factor in figure quality. The same data can make a very different impression depending on how it is saved.

| | Bitmap | Vector |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stored as | Pixels | Lines, shapes and text defined by mathematical coordinates |
| When resized | Blurs when enlarged; text smears when shrunk | Stays sharp at any size |
| Strengths | Quick and easy to produce | Line weight, font size and color stay editable; suited to publication |
| Common formats | JPG, PNG, BMP | PDF, AI, EMF, SVG |
| Best for | Photos and quick, temporary visuals | Graphs, schematics, data labels |
| Final submission | Not recommended | Recommended |

The figures that explain your core findings, such as Figures 1 to 3, should always be prepared as vectors.

## A practical workflow: MATLAB, PowerPoint, Photoshop

Many people assume figures must be drawn in professional software such as Adobe Illustrator. In practice, PowerPoint and Photoshop are enough for most high-quality figures, and PowerPoint is far more capable at planning and editing them than you might expect.

**1. Generate the graph.** Plot your raw data in MATLAB, GraphPad or a similar program. In MATLAB, copy the graph with **Copy as Vector**.

**2. Assemble in PowerPoint.** Paste the graph in, right-click and choose **Ungroup**, and every line, label and background becomes editable. Use **Align** and **Distribute** to tidy the layout, delete anything unnecessary, and add simple boxes or shapes to explain conditions or timelines between panels. This makes PowerPoint especially good for multipanel figures. Save the result as a PDF and it keeps its vector quality.

**3. Finish in Photoshop.** Copy the figure from PowerPoint or open the PDF, crop away excess margins, set the color mode (RGB or CMYK) and the dpi, and save as a TIFF, choosing to discard layers so the file meets journal requirements.

One caution: opening a vector file in Photoshop turns it into a bitmap. Keep your master figures as PDF or AI files, and convert to TIFF or other formats only when a journal asks for them. Throughout, remember that a paper figure has to be easy to read, not merely nice to look at. Crisp lines, legible fonts and a clear color scheme are what count.

## Design principles: the clearest figure is the strongest

A good figure is not the flashiest one. It is the one a viewer understands at once. Three principles get you most of the way there.

**Simplify.** Remove anything unrelated to the results, such as decorative backgrounds or unnecessary numbers. Too many overlapping lines or conditions weaken the message, and too many colors confuse it, so stick to three or four at most. Leave statistically insignificant conditions out of the figure; if they are needed, move them to the supplementary material.

**Clarify.** Always include scale bars and color bars. Give every label (axis names, units, conditions) the same font size and make it easy to see. Prefer plain wording to jargon: "Signal intensity (normalized)" can be clearer than "Relative fluorescence."

**Emphasize.** Give your key result the most space and put reference images or comparison samples in small insets. Set the condition you want to highlight apart with a darker color or thicker line; in a control-versus-treatment plot, draw the treatment line bolder and in a stronger color.

A few finishing details make a noticeable difference:

| Element | Tip |
| --- | --- |
| Font | Use one font and size throughout the paper; Arial and Helvetica are preferred |
| Alignment | Space all graph elements evenly and align them on a common axis |
| Layout | Keep every figure a consistent size, either square or landscape |
| Panel labels | Place lowercase labels, (a), (b), (c), consistently at the top left |

The aim is to make the reader understand, not simply to show them something.

## Build a collection of reference figures

One of the fastest ways to improve is to collect well-made figures and imitate them, the way writers copy out good sentences to sharpen their prose. When a figure in a strong paper catches your eye, capture it, save it to a PDF or a slide deck, and jot down what works: "the color combination stands out," "the inset placement is clean." As the collection grows, study:

- **Color:** background contrast, accent colors, how the colormap is built
- **Fonts and labels:** size, position, how units are written
- **Panel layout:** how panels a, b and c are arranged and separated
- **Emphasis:** how key conditions stand out through line weight or color
- **Information load:** how much a single figure tries to convey

Then practice. Borrow the structure of a figure you admire and apply it to your own data, or try several ways of visualizing the same result. Over time, you learn to build the story of a paper around its figures.

## Every figure shows how you work

Readers notice whether a figure is orderly before they weigh its data: a cluttered one suggests an overly complicated experimental design or a paper rushed out before the results were sorted, while a clean, precise one signals a study organized from the start and worth reading in full.

Good figures grow out of a few questions. How can I show this result most clearly? Can I make complex data persuasive at a glance? Will a reviewer understand it and move on? A figure is a researcher's language, and it says a great deal about how organized your work is, how logically you think and how seriously you take it.

If you want to put these habits to work on a paper of your own, the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) brings small groups of students together with visiting professors from US and UK universities to carry out real research and write it up in English. Part 4 of this series turns to writing the results and discussion.
